claim: Álvaro Siza, Pritzker Architecture Prize 1992
value: Born 25 June 1933 in Matosinhos; studied at the Porto School of Architecture 1949-1955; first built works four houses in Matosinhos; own office in Porto from 1954; taught at the University of Porto from 1966, tenured professor in 1976; works include the Leça swimming pool (Matosinhos), the Serralves Museum and the Porto Faculty of Architecture, the Borges & Irmão bank in Vila do Conde (1982-86), the Malagueira housing in Évora (from 1977) and the rebuilding of the Chiado after the 1988 fire The Pritzker page dates the Boa Nova restaurant (Matosinhos) 1963 and the Leça pool 1966; Malagueira: commissioned in 1977 by the Évora city government after the revolution, 1200 low-cost one- and two-storey row houses, all with courtyards; quotes Casabella (July 1986) on 'the heroic spirit of modern architecture'.
source_title: The Pritzker Architecture Prize, Alvaro Siza, 1992 Laureate

claim: Eduardo Souto de Moura, Pritzker Architecture Prize 2011
value: Born in Porto in 1952; worked five years for Álvaro Siza as a student; own office since 1980; second Portuguese laureate after Siza (1992); works include the Braga Municipal Stadium (2004), the Burgo Tower in Porto (2007), the Paula Rego museum (2008), the Porto Cultural Centre (1991) and Santa Maria do Bouro (1989-97) Biography: began at the Porto School of Fine Arts studying sculpture and credits a meeting with Donald Judd in Zurich for the switch to architecture; Braga: nearly 1.5 million cubic yards of granite blasted and crushed for the concrete, a hundred-foot granite face closing one end, 'a drama to break down the mountain and make concrete from the stone'; Bouro: 12th-century monastery, walls over four feet thick; jury: work 'of our time but also carries echoes of architectural traditions'; Paula Rego museum: the painter chose him, he chose the site (a fenced-off forest with an open space), red concrete in opposition to the green forest.
source_title: The Pritzker Architecture Prize, Eduardo Souto de Moura, 2011 Laureate

claim: Creation of the Companhia Geral da Agricultura das Vinhas do Alto Douro and of the Douro Demarcated Region
value: 10 September 1756; the charter that created the Companhia and the Demarcated Region is considered the first appellation of origin in the world; rules included a register of vineyard plots, maximum sale quantities, prices by quality checked by the Companhia's staff and a ban on additives that changed the wine; the charter also rebalanced the finances of the Douro landowners and of the merchants established in Gaia and Porto; Pombal drew on his years as ambassador in London and Vienna Before 1756: wines of many origins were doctored to pass as Port (elderberry for colour, darker Spanish wine, sugar to hide poor brandy); crisis around 1750; in 1754 the English did not buy wine from the growers; France defined the appellation d'origine only in the first quarter of the 20th century.
source_title: IVDP, Vinho do Porto, História

claim: Douro and Port wine milestones
value: 1757-1761 Pombaline demarcations (first demarcation); first Vintage in a Christie's auction catalogue in 1768; 1788 Marian demarcations; 1792 the Cachão da Valeira cleared, the Douro navigable to Spain; 2001 UNESCO World Heritage (Alto Douro Wine Region); Museu do Douro created by Lei 125/97 as a territory museum, its seat in Peso da Régua in the former Companhia building, opened 20 Dec 2008 The Christie's line reads '1765 Primeiro Vintage a aparecer num catálogo de leilões da Christies, em 1768'. In the 18th century English, Dutch, German and other northern European merchants settled in Porto ran the wine trade; the Carrapatelo dam (1964-1971), first of five on the Portuguese Douro (Carrapatelo, Régua, Valeira, Pocinho, Crestuma/Lever), ended the rabelo boats' centuries-long carriage of wine casks to Vila Nova de Gaia, replaced by the train and then tanker lorries.

claim: The royal family in Cascais from 1870
value: From 1870 King Luís and Queen Maria Pia set up the royal residence in the governor's houses of the Cidadela, adapted to a design by Joaquim Possidónio Narciso da Silva; in 1878, on the day Prince Carlos was given the schooner Nautilus for his 15th birthday, Cascais saw the first electric lighting trial in Portugal; King Luís died in the Paço de Cascais in 1889; King Carlos set up Portugal's first marine biology laboratory there in 1896; fishermen had to give bathers part of the Praia da Ribeira (Praia dos Pescadores), from where King Carlos promoted sailing, rowing and swimming and Cascais became the most prestigious regatta ground in Portugal; the Praia da Rainha (once Boca do Asno) was Queen Maria Pia's choice for the princes' sea baths, and there Queen Amélia saved a fisherman from drowning in 1900; King Carlos is remembered as the founder of Portuguese oceanography; the route includes the Casa das Histórias Paula Rego; after 1910 the palace received the presidents of the Republic, official residence of Óscar Carmona 1928-1945; restored 2007-2008, today an official residence of the President, with guided visits by the Museu da Presidência da República The route's tide gauge (Marégrafo de Cascais): installed 1882, linked to King Carlos's oceanographic laboratory, moved about 30 m in 1900; a float in a well linked to a high-precision clock and a horizontal cylinder that records the float's movements as a graph; still works, visits by appointment. The Praia da Rainha cove was once called Boca do Asno. Brochure photograph: King Carlos rowing (and smoking) in front of the Casino da Praia, 1900. Statue of King Carlos by Luís Valadares (2008), aboard the yacht Amélia with binoculars.
source_title: Câmara Municipal de Cascais, Rota D. Carlos em Cascais (brochure)
